units.title: Shapes of Simple Molecules and crystals
units.intro: By the end: VSEPR assumptions, electron-pair vs molecular shape, lattice / unit cell, crystal systems and types.

f1.title: If every pair is a bond, shape name = electron-pair name.

cards.title: 1.1 Shapes of simple molecules
body: Lewis structures of molecules show the shared electron pairs (bonding pairs) as short lines or as pair of dots between the atoms, and the unshared pairs or nonbonding pairs (or lone pairs) as pairs of dots on individual atoms.
Blow up all four balloons to the same size.
Electron pairs repel each other because they are like charges.
Electron pairs in the valence shell of an atom tend to orient themselves so that their total energy is minimized.
Repulsive force decreases with an increase of inter-pair angle.

cards.title: 1.1 Shapes of simple molecules
body: Draw Lewis structures for O₂ and F₂. How many bonding pairs? How many lone pairs on each F in F₂?
Peek
O₂: double bond (2 shared pairs), 2 lone pairs on each O. F₂: single bond, 3 lone pairs on each F. Lewis drawings are flat; real molecules are 3-D — that is why we need VSEPR.

cards.title: VSEPR in one breath
body: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion: electron pairs around a central atom push apart and sit as far from each other as they can.
*Electron-pair geometry* counts **all** pairs (bonds + lone pairs). *Molecular shape* counts only atoms (lone pairs still push, but you don’t “see” them in the shape name).

cards.title: 2 pairs → linear
body: 180°. BeH₂, CO₂. All atoms in a straight line.

cards.title: 3 pairs → trigonal planar
body: 120°. BF₃. Flat triangle.

cards.title: 4 pairs → tetrahedral
body: 109.5°. CH₄. Central atom in the middle of a pyramid with a triangular base.

cards.title: Lone pairs change the name
body: H₂O: 4 pairs (2 bond + 2 lone) → electron geometry tetrahedral, *shape bent* (~104.5°). NH₃: 3 bond + 1 lone → *trigonal pyramidal*.

cards.title: If every pair is a bond, shape name = electron-pair name.
Mnemonic — lone pairs are bullies
body: Lone pair–lone pair repulsion > lone pair–bond pair > bond–bond. That is why water is squeezed from 109.5° to about 104.5°.
Why it matters: if H₂O were linear it would not be a liquid at room temperature — polarity (and life) depends on the bent shape.

cards.title: Key takeaways
body:
- VSEPR: pairs repel; lone pairs bully angles.
- Shape ≠ electron geometry if lone pairs exist.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The transition in molecular shape that occurs when boron trifluoride ($$\text{BF}_3$$) reacts with a fluoride ion ($$\text{F}^-$$) to yield the tetrafluoroborate anion ($$\text{BF}_4^-$$) is from:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the reactant shape**
In $$\text{BF}_3$$, Boron has 3 valence electrons and forms 3 bonds with fluorine. It has 3 electron domains, giving it a **trigonal planar** shape.

**Step 2: Analyze the product shape**
In $$\text{BF}_4^-$$, the boron atom coordinates with a fourth fluoride ion. Boron now has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs. Under VSEPR, 4 domains adopt a **tetrahedral** s

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following terms describes the smallest repeating unit in a three-dimensional crystal lattice?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall definitions of crystalline structures**
A crystal lattice is an infinite pattern of points in space.

**Step 2: Identify the fundamental building block**
The smallest unit of a crystal that, when translated repeatedly in three dimensions, reconstructs the entire crystal lattice is defined as the unit cell.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct term is the **unit cell**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the predicted bond angle in a molecule with a perfectly trigonal planar electron-pair geometry?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the geometric parameters**
A trigonal planar electron-pair geometry consists of three electron domains distributed symmetrically around a central atom.

**Step 2: Calculate the ideal angular spacing**
To minimize repulsion in a two-dimensional plane, the three domains split a full circle equally:
$$\text{Bond Angle} = \frac{360^\circ}{3} = 120^\circ$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
T

cards.title: 1.2 Crystals
body: A **crystal** is a solid whose particles sit in a repeating 3-D pattern. That pattern is the **crystal lattice**. The smallest repeating box that still has the full symmetry is the **unit cell**.
**Coordination number** = how many nearest neighbours touch a particle. In NaCl each Na⁺ has 6 Cl⁻ neighbours (and vice versa).
Seven crystal systems (by unit-cell edge lengths and angles): cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, hexagonal, trigonal (rhombohedral), monoclinic, triclinic.

cards.title: Mnemonic — C TOH TMT
body: “Cute Tigers Often Hug Tiny Meek Tigers” — Cubic, Tetragonal, Orthorhombic, Hexagonal, Trigonal, Monoclinic, Triclinic.

cards.title: Four types of crystal (by force) · Ionic
body: Ions + strong electrostatic force. NaCl, CsCl. Hard, high m.p., conduct when molten or dissolved.

cards.title: Covalent / macromolecular
body: The whole crystal is one giant molecule. Diamond, quartz, graphite. Very high m.p.

cards.title: Molecular
body: Molecules held by van der Waals or H-bonds. Ice, iodine, solid neon. Soft, low m.p.

cards.title: Metallic
body: Metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons. Cu, Fe. Malleable, conduct heat and electricity.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Exam trick: “giant covalent” almost always means diamond / SiO₂. “Conducts only when molten” = ionic.

cards.title: Key takeaways
body: - Four crystal types by force.

cards.title: 1.2.1 What is a crystal?
body: Is this a two-dimensional or three-dimensional arrangement.
Solids can be either crystalline or noncrsytalline (amorphous).
The regularly spaced pattern resulting when atoms, molecules or ions are arranged to form a crystal is called a crystal lattice.
In discussing the structure of crystals, it becomes important to differentiate between crystal lattice, which is the repetition pattern, and the unit cell, which is repeated.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Types of Crystals
body: Sodium chloride and cesium chloride are examples of ionic crystals.
The constituent particles of sodium chloride are sodium and chloride ions.
The structure of sodium chloride is given in Fig.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: How many bonding pairs of atoms are attached to the central carbon atom in a tetrahedral methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$) molecule?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write down the molecular composition**
Methane has the formula $$\text{CH}_4$$.

**Step 2: Determine valence bonds**
Carbon is in Group 14 and has 4 valence electrons. Hydrogen has 1 valence electron. Carbon forms four single covalent bonds, one with each hydrogen atom, leaving no lone pairs.

**Step 3: Final Result**
There are exactly **$$4$$** bonding pairs.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven primary crystal systems?
cards.why:
**Step 1: List the seven crystal systems**
The seven systems are: cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, rhombohedral, monoclinic, triclinic, and hexagonal.

**Step 2: Identify the outlier**
'Square planar' is a molecular geometry describing the spatial arrangement of atoms around a single central atom (such as $$\text{XeF}_4$$), not a 3D unit cell crystal system.

**Step 3: Final Result**
**Square planar** is not a crystal system.

glossary.meaning: A solid whose particles sit in a repeating 3-D pattern.
How many nearest neighbours touch a particle.
A central atom is an atom to which all other atoms in the molecule are bonded.
Molecular geometry refers to the spatial arrangement of atoms in a molecule.
You know that molecular shape is the spatial arrangement of atomic nuclei that is determined by the location of its atoms, while ignoring the orientation of the non-bonding pairs.

tips.text: Molecular geometry refers to the spatial arrangement of atoms in a molecule.

The VSEPR theory is a simple model for predicting molecular geometries. It is based on the idea that electron pairs around a central atom are arranged as far apart as possible to minimize electron-pair repulsion.
There are two kinds of electron pair: bonding and non-bonding.
The geometry of a molecule is the same as the geometry of the electron pairs if all the electron pairs around the central atom are bonding.
If the electron pairs around the central atom are both bonding and nonbonding, the geometry of a molecule is determined by the direction of the bonding pairs.

similar.q: Amorphous solid is characterized by  A) melting at a specific temperature.  B) definite geometrical shape.  C) lack of well-defined shape.  D) flat faces.  E) None of the above.
similar.a: C. lack of well-defined shape. — So it has no definite geometrical shape or flat faces and softens over a range of temperature instead of a sharp melting point. Answer: C.

similar.q: The solid substance in which the atoms, ions or molecules are arranged in an orderly manner is called  A) crystal lattice.  B) crystal.  C) coordination number.  D) unit cell.  E) amorphous.
similar.a: B. crystal. — The crystal lattice is the regularly spaced pattern (not the substance); the unit cell is the smallest repeating unit; an amorphous solid has no regular arrangement. Answer: B.

questions.q: Which type of crystal has the lowest melting point?
why: Molecular crystals (e.g. ice, solid neon, iodine) are held together only by weak intermolecular forces (van der Waals, hydrogen bonds).
Ionic (strong electrostatic attraction), covalent network (covalent bonds throughout, e.g. diamond) and metallic crystals need much more energy to melt.
Answer: C.
